source_title: Is America More Divided Than Ever?

context_before.text: This episode has been brought to you
by our super generous supporters on Patreon.
So as many of you are probably aware,
we recently had an election for president
of the United States of America.
And the reaction to the result has been mixed.
This song.
And it wasn't just the result of the election.
This whole election process over the past year and a half
has been ugly.
And the rhetoric seemed to be much more divisive than any other
election that I can remember.
And there's been this idea going around
that America is now more divided than ever.
But is this true?
Are we really that deeply divided?
Or is there another possible explanation?
When people say that America is divided,
what are they actually talking about?
Most of you are probably familiar with this electoral map
by now, the good old red states and blue states.
And as you are probably aware,
if you zoom in past the state boundaries,
what you'll find is that the red and blue divide
is actually much more pronounced from county to county
rather than between the states themselves.
This reflects an increasing trend
that has been going on for decades now.

context_after.text: And this divide is even more extreme in big cities
and especially rural and remote areas.
So when it comes to voting for one of the two major parties,
there does seem to be a growing geographic divide.
But what about our beliefs and values?
Is there an ideological divide as well?
In 1994, the Pew Research Center began a survey
where they asked a large sample group of Americans
10 ideological questions to determine
their political values and then ranked them
on a scale of consistently liberal
to consistently conservative.
This chart shows the results from 1994.
The blue represents the Democrats
and the red is Republicans.
As you can see, there's some red and blue areas
off to the sides, but there is a large overlapping region
in the middle.
As time goes on, you could see the red and blue blobs
shift along the spectrum.
And for some reason, in the past decade or so,
the two blobs have very noticeably drifted apart.
The blues have become bluer, the red's redder,
and the moderate overlapping part
has shrunk significantly.
Another study by the Pew Research Center found
that in 2016, 58% of Republicans
have a very unfavorable impression
of the Democratic Party, up from 46% in 2014
and just 32% in 2008.
The Democrats have followed a similar trajectory
over the years.
Currently, 55% find Republicans very unfavorable.
What's even more alarming, though,
is that the same study found that 45% of Republicans
and 41% of Democrats actually see the other side
as a threat to the nation's well-being.
This is a sharp increase, even, from just two years ago.
So what's actually going on here?
What's with all the distrust and animosity?
Well, interestingly enough, despite the fact
that voters' allegiances to their parties seems strong,
there's a lot of evidence to suggest
that people are fed up with the whole system.
A recent poll by Jen Foward showed
that only 28% of young adults overall
feel that the two major parties do a good job
of representing the American people,
and there's been a sharp increase over the past few years
of people who identify as independents.
But if Americans are so unified
in their dissatisfaction with politics,
then how do we explain this?
Well, let's take a look at how this chart was created.
Here are the 10 ideological prompts that were given
to determine where a person fell
along the liberal conservative spectrum.
Some of these prompts are classic big government
versus small government situations,
like government is almost always wasteful and inefficient,
versus government often does a better job
than people give it credit for.
But as you go further down the list,
you start to see prompts that are more about social issues,
like racial discrimination,
and whether or not homosexuality should be discouraged
or accepted by society.
Americans are definitely divided on these issues,
but is it really the even split
that we can see in this chart?
Public opinion of gay marriage, for example,
has consistently increased over the past decade
across all age groups,
even while the political parties have become more polarized.
And according to this chart,
most Americans now believe
that stricter environmental regulations are worth the cost.
These are the same questions
that the Pew Research Center has been asking since 1994,
and in many ways they do seem to reflect
the platforms of the two parties, but do they reflect us?
Could it be possible that the divide in our country
is not so much about the issues,
but about something that's more connected
to human behavior?
When I was a kid, politics were not that big of a deal.
In my neighborhood, you could vote Republican one year
and then flip and vote Democrat for the next election.
We could make jokes about our neighbor's ultra-conservative
or liberal hippie refrigerator magnets,
but we still went to their Christmas party every year.
It wasn't like we actually thought
that their political beliefs represented
a threat to democracy,
but this year, the vibe of the election just felt different.
In fact, it kind of felt like a sporting event.
Tonight, a must-see debate.
Two bitter rivals going head-to-head for the first time.
Both candidates fighting to seize momentum
in the final stretch of a close and polarizing race.
Two nominees, one stage, and America's future.
The crowds seem to be more energized than usual.
There were playoffs followed by the main event.
And then of course, you've got your team mascots
and colors, and if you walked around your neighborhood
just before the election, there's a good chance
that your neighbors were all displaying
the same team banners,
not unlike being in Chicago
when the Cubs were in the World Series.
People like to support their team.
It's called tribalism.
It's a way of thinking or behaving
in which people are excessively loyal to their tribe.
But in terms of human behavior,
your tribe could be a lot of things.
It could be the company you work for,
your school, family, local sports team,
or your political party.
When people see themselves as part of a tribe,
they will often go out of their way
to defend the beliefs of their tribe,
regardless of whether or not they're right or wrong.
This could be due to our human desire
for acceptance from within our group
and something that social psychologists call
naive realism.
Naive realism is the human tendency to believe
that we see the world around us objectively.
And anyone who disagrees with us
is either uninformed, irrational, or biased.
This means that if we think that a person
or even a media outlet is part of the other tribe,
that we are far less likely to seriously consider
anything that they have to say,
which is something that I am admittedly guilty of a lot.
In fact, if you present someone with factual evidence
that discredits their tribal beliefs,
you will often have the opposite effect
of actually strengthening their beliefs.
And in this modern era of talking points,
buzzwords, and hashtags,
it's becoming increasingly easy
to quickly identify someone who's in your tribe
and someone who's not.
If we spend enough time with our tribe,
we're also likely to experience something
called group polarization,
which is the tendency for a group to make decisions
that are more extreme
than the initial inclination of its members.
And because more and more people get their news
and information today from social media platforms
like Facebook, we're far more likely
to only be exposed to ideas
that reinforce our tribal beliefs.
Some of this may be a result of Facebook's algorithms,
an effect which is known as the filter bubble,
but it's also due to who we decide to be friends with
and our natural tendency to seek news from sources
that support our worldview.
So looking back at this chart,
is this the result of a profound ideological divide
or two tribes retreating deeper into their own camps?
It's hard to say for sure.
I know there were definitely times in America's past
that we were ideologically divided,
and I think this isn't as bad as some of those times,
but it's still cause for concern.
Democracy functions by people with different beliefs
coming together and making compromises
and finding common ground.
That's how we progress as a society.
And if we can't even talk to each other,
then there's no way we're gonna be able to do that.
Government isn't going to be able to function,
and we're just gonna be angry and resentful.
But I don't think it's completely hopeless.
There are ways even to change the political process
that might make the tribal effect less powerful.
For example, the state of Maine just voted yes
on a referendum for something called ranked choice voting,
which is a way of electing government officials
where you have to rank them
instead of just voting yes or no.
So this system works if there are three or more candidates.
It eliminates the possibility of somebody winning
with less than 50% of the vote.
It has been shown to discourage negative campaign ads,
and it could even give third-party candidates a shot.
I don't know what the solution is
to this problem in our country,
but in times like these,
I am often reminded of this quote
from the great wizard, Albus Dumbledore.
We are only as strong as we are united,
as weak as we are divided.
Thank you.
So what do you guys think?
Can we get past the supposed divide in our country?
And how can we do that?
And please, if you're gonna say something political,
you know, just be respectful about it.
If you liked this video,
please click like and subscribe.
And if you wanna support our show,
head on over to Patreon and consider becoming a supporter.
Our show is now completely 100% funded
by our Patreon supporters,
like these awesome people down here.
We couldn't do it without you guys.
Thanks.
